title: The HTTP ETags Handbook: How Browsers Know a File Hasn’t Changed Without Re-Downloading It
partialText:
Refresh a webpage. Your browser sends a request. The server replies:

“I’m not sending it.”

No body. No JSON. No HTML. And yet the page still renders perfectly, with what looks like the latest data. That shouldn’t be possible — but it happens on almost every site you use, thousands of times a day.

Open your browser’s Developer Tools and refresh almost any modern website. In the Network tab, you’ll probably see something like this:

GET /api/profile

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified

At first glance, nothing looks unusual. The page loads, the data appears on the screen, and everything works as expected. Most developers see this response hundreds of times and never think about it again.

But look closer. The server just refused to send the resource, and the browser was completely fine with that.

How? If the server didn’t send the resource, where did the browser get it? And even more interesting, how did the server know the browser already had the correct version?

Did the server remember your last request? Does it keep a record for every browser that visits your website? If a million users refresh the same page, does the server remember a million different copies? Or is something much smarter happening behind the scenes?

These questions lead to one of the most elegant ideas in the HTTP protocol. And surprisingly, the idea isn’t really about caching. It’s about agreement — specifically, how two completely independent computers, a browser and a server, can agree they’re looking at exactly the same version of a resource without sending the resource itself.

That might sound like a small optimization. In reality, it’s a fundamental problem in distributed systems, and one that every modern website solves thousands or even millions of times every day.

What You’ll Learn

By the end of this handbook, you’ll understand not only what an ETag is, but also why HTTP needed it, how browsers and servers use it to avoid unnecessary downloads, how to implement it yourself in real code, how it prevents lost updates when two people edit the same resource, how it relates to Last-Modified and Cache-Control, and what happens when this simple idea meets load balancers, CDNs, and globally distributed systems.

Prerequisites

You don’t need much to follow along. A basic understanding of how HTTP requests and responses work — a browser sends a request, a server sends back a status code and a body — is enough. Familiarity with JSON and a little backend experience will help, but every concept is explained from first principles.

Table of Contents

  • The Problem Nobody Could Ignore
  • Every Resource Needs an Identity
  • The Conversation Between the Browser and the Server
  • Where ETags Come From and How Servers Generate Them
  • Why Servers Stay Stateless
  • Generating ETags in Practice
  • Strong ETags vs Weak ETags
  • Beyond Caching: Using ETags for Safe Updates
  • ETag, Last-Modified, and Cache-Control
  • ETags in Distributed Systems
  • Common Mistakes and Pitfalls
  • When Should You Use ETags?
  • The Mental Model to Remember

The Problem Nobody Could Ignore

Let’s forget about ETags for a moment and imagine HTTP didn’t have them. Every time you opened a webpage, your browser would request every resource from the server. Refresh the page, and it would request everything again. Open the same page five seconds later, and it would request everything again — even if absolutely nothing had changed.

Here’s a simple example. A user opens their profile page, and the browser sends a request:

GET /api/profile

The server reads the latest data from the database and returns the response:

{
  "id": 10,
  "name": "Tanzim",
  "followers": 1284
}

Assume the response is 120 KB. The browser downloads it, renders the page, and everyone is happy.

Five seconds later, the user presses Refresh. The browser sends exactly the same request again:

GET /api/profile

Now stop and think. Nothing changed — the user didn’t update their profile, and nobody changed the database. The response is still exactly the same. Should the server really send another 120 KB?

Technically it can. But should it? If it does, here’s what happens:

Request #1                 Request #2 (5 seconds later)
Browser                    Browser
    │                          │
    ▼                          ▼
Server                     Server
    │                          │
120 KB                     120 KB again
    ▼                          ▼
Browser                    Browser

The browser already has an identical copy, and the server already knows the data hasn’t changed. Yet both machines spend time transferring the exact same bytes across the network again.

For one user, this isn’t a problem. For one million users, it becomes expensive.

Imagine a news website. Most visitors refresh the homepage several times throughout the day, and most of those refreshes don’t introduce any new articles. Without a better solution, the server keeps sending the same HTML, the same CSS, the same JavaScript, and the same API responses over and over again.

That creates unnecessary work everywhere. The network transfers data that already exists on the user’s computer, the server spends CPU time generating responses it has generated before, and the browser downloads data it already owns — all while the user waits for information that hasn’t changed.

The obvious answer might be: “Then don’t ask the server again.” That sounds reasonable, until something actually changes.

Suppose another user updates their profile picture, or a new notification arrives, or today’s weather changes. Now the browser’s local copy is no longer correct. If the browser never contacts the server again, it keeps showing outdated information forever.

So we’ve discovered two opposite problems:

Always download everything        Never contact the server
        │                                 │
        ├── Always correct                ├── Extremely fast
        └── Wastes bandwidth              └── Eventually shows stale data

Neither solution is acceptable. One wastes resources, the other sacrifices correctness. What you really need is something in between — a way for the browser to ask a much smaller question.

Not: “Please send me the entire resource again.” Instead:

“Has this resource changed since the last time I downloaded it?”

If the answer is No, the browser can safely reuse its local copy. If the answer is Yes, then — and only then — does it need to download the latest version.

That sounds simple, but it introduces a much deeper question. How can the browser and the server determine whether they’re talking about the same version of a resource without comparing the entire resource itself?

That simple question is where the real story begins.

Every Resource Needs an Identity

The browser has a problem, and the server has a problem too. The browser wants to know whether its local copy is still valid, and the server wants to answer that question without sending the entire resource again.

At first, this seems impossible. How can two computers compare something without exchanging it? The answer is surprisingly simple: they don’t compare the resource. They compare its identity.

Think about a document in Google Docs. You don’t ask your teammate, “Read the entire document to me so I can check whether it’s the same.” Instead, you ask something much smaller: “Are you still looking at Version 12?” If they answer “Yes,” the conversation ends. No one reads the document again, because the version number tells both people they’re talking about exactly the same document.

HTTP uses the same idea. Instead of comparing an entire response, it gives every version of a resource a unique identity. That identity is called an ETag.

An ETag is a unique identifier that represents one specific version of a resource.

Notice what that definition doesn’t say. It doesn’t say an ETag contains the resource — it doesn’t. It doesn’t say an ETag is a cache — it isn’t. It simply answers one question: “Which version of this resource are you looking at?”

Here’s the flow. The browser downloads the profile once, and along with the response, the server also sends its identity:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "v37"

{
  "id": 10,
  "name": "Tanzim",
  "followers": 1284
}

Now the browser knows something very important: the copy it’s storing is Version 37.

Here’s the interesting part. The browser doesn’t care how the server created "v37". Maybe it's a version number, maybe a timestamp, maybe a hash, maybe something else entirely. The browser treats it as an opaque value — it never tries to understand the ETag, it simply remembers it.

That’s an important detail, because many developers assume an ETag must be a hash. It doesn’t have to be. As far as HTTP is concerned, an ETag is just an identifier.

So the browser stores two things together:

Browser Cache
├── Response Body
└── ETag: "v37"

Now think about what happens when the user refreshes the page. The browser already has the response, and it already knows its identity. So instead of saying “Please send me the profile again,” it asks a much smarter question:

“I already have Version 37. Is Version 37 still the latest?”

Everything suddenly becomes much simpler. The browser no longer needs the entire response just to discover nothing has changed — it only needs the server to answer yes or no.

That tiny shift in thinking is what makes HTTP cache validation so efficient. The browser isn’t asking for data anymore. It’s asking whether its version is still current. And that’s exactly where two HTTP headers enter the conversation: ETag and If-None-Match.

The Conversation Between the Browser and the Server

Now that every resource has an identity, the browser and the server finally have a common language. Instead of repeatedly transferring the same resource, they can simply compare its identity. Let’s follow one request from beginning to end.

Step 1 — The browser requests the resource for the first time

The user opens their profile page. The browser has never seen this resource before, so it has nothing stored locally, and it sends a normal HTTP request:

GET /api/profile

At this point, the server behaves exactly as it always has. It reads the latest data from the database, builds the JSON response, and prepares to send it back. But this time it does one extra thing: before sending the response, it attaches the resource’s identity.

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "v37"

{
  "id": 10,
  "name": "Tanzim",
  "followers": 1284
}

The browser now receives two things: the JSON body, which it uses to render the page, and the ETag, which it quietly stores alongside it. As before, the browser doesn’t try to understand what "v37" means — it simply remembers it.

Step 2 — The user refreshes the page

A few seconds later, the user presses Refresh. The browser already has the response stored locally, and more importantly, it also remembers the resource’s identity. Instead of pretending it knows the resource is still valid, it asks the server to confirm:

GET /api/profile
If-None-Match: "v37"

This is the browser saying: “I already have Version 37. Is that still the latest version?”

Notice what the browser didn’t do. It didn’t send the old JSON back to the server, and it didn’t upload the cached response. It only sent a tiny identifier, and that single header is enough for the server to understand exactly which version the browser already has.

Step 3 — The server compares versions

The server receives the request and asks a simple question: “What is the current version of this resource?” Suppose the current version is still v37. Both sides are talking about the same version, so nothing has changed and there's no reason to send the entire response again. The server replies with:

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified

That’s all. No JSON, no HTML, no response body — just a small HTTP response saying, “Your copy is still correct.”

Step 4 — The browser reuses its local copy

When the browser receives 304 Not Modified, it doesn't display an empty page. Instead, it opens the cached response it stored earlier and renders the page using the existing data. From the user's perspective, everything works exactly as if the server had sent the response again. The difference is that almost no data crossed the network.

Here’s the whole first-request-then-refresh conversation as a sequence:

What happens if the resource changes?

Now imagine another user updates the profile, so the current version becomes v38. The browser still has v37. When it refreshes, it sends:

GET /api/profile
If-None-Match: "v37"

This time the server compares v37 (browser) against v38 (current), and they don't match. The browser's copy is outdated, so the server sends a completely new response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "v38"

{
  "id": 10,
  "name": "Tanzim",
  "followers": 1285
}

The browser replaces both the cached response and the old ETag. The next time it refreshes, it will send If-None-Match: "v38", and the conversation repeats.

The whole decision the server makes on every validation request looks like this:

This entire exchange happens in just a few milliseconds, and neither side performs anything magical. The browser simply remembers which version it has, and the server simply checks whether that version is still current. Once you see the protocol as a conversation instead of a collection of HTTP headers, the behavior becomes surprisingly intuitive.

Why this conversation saves so much

At first glance, this conversation doesn’t seem particularly impressive. The browser sends an identifier, the server compares it, and if nothing changed it replies with 304 Not Modified. Just a few bytes travel across the network. It almost feels too simple.

But this tiny exchange solves a surprisingly expensive problem. Imagine the profile response is 120 KB and a user refreshes the page ten times. Without cache validation, the server sends the full body every time:

Without validation          With ETag validation
120 KB                      120 KB   ← first request only
120 KB                      304
120 KB                      304
120 KB                      304
120 KB                      304
120 KB                      304
120 KB                      304
120 KB                      304
120 KB                      304
120 KB                      304
─────                       ─────
1.2 MB transferred          ~120 KB transferred

Only the first request transfers the full response. Every request after that sends only a tiny confirmation that the browser’s copy is still valid.

The browser doesn’t become faster because it suddenly learned a new trick. It becomes faster because it avoids unnecessary work. The server avoids rebuilding and transmitting identical responses, the browser avoids downloading data it already has, and the network avoids carrying the same bytes repeatedly. Everyone wins.

This is why ETags are used everywhere. Every time your browser requests a profile, a blog post, an image, a CSS file, or a JavaScript bundle, the same conversation can happen. Sometimes the resource changes and sometimes it doesn’t — and ETags make that decision inexpensive.

But one mystery remains. Throughout these examples we’ve used an ETag like "v37". Where did v37 come from? Did the server invent it? Is it a database version, a timestamp, or a cryptographic hash? And if the server is stateless, how does it know what ETag to compare against when the next request arrives? Those questions take us from understanding the HTTP protocol into understanding how servers actually implement it.

Where ETags Come From and How Servers Generate Them

Earlier, the server responded with ETag: "v37", and later the browser sent If-None-Match: "v37". The server compared the versions and immediately knew whether the browser's copy was still valid. But where did "v37" come from?

If you’ve never looked into ETags before, you might imagine the server keeps a giant table somewhere:

/profile        → v37
/posts          → v18
/settings       → v42
/products/100   → v91

When a request arrives, the server looks up the resource, finds its ETag, and compares it with the value sent by the browser. It sounds reasonable. But in most production systems, that’s not what happens.

Why? Because modern web servers are usually stateless. We’ll explore statelessness in detail later, but here’s the important idea for now: a server should be able to handle any request without remembering previous requests. That means the server doesn’t usually keep a giant list of ETags in memory. Instead, it recreates the ETag whenever it needs it.

This is an important shift in thinking. The browser remembers the ETag, the server recreates the current ETag, and then it compares the two:

Browser                          Server
├── Response Body                ├── Recreate current ETag
└── ETag: "v37"    ──refresh──▶  └── Compare with If-None-Match
    GET /profile
    If-None-Match: "v37"

Notice something. The browser never asks, “How did you create this ETag?” And the server never explains. As far as HTTP is concerned, an ETag is just an identifier. It could be a version number, a timestamp, a cryptographic hash, file metadata, or any other value that uniquely identifies the current version of the resource.

The browser treats the ETag like a sealed envelope. It receives it, stores it, and later sends it back exactly as it received it. The only component that understands what the ETag means is the server that created it.

This design gives servers enormous flexibility. One application might use a version column from the database, another might hash the entire response, and another might generate ETags from file metadata. All of them are valid, because HTTP never defines how an ETag must be created. It only requires that the identifier changes whenever the resource changes.

So the real question isn’t “What is an ETag?” — we’ve already answered that. The new question is: “If the server can choose any strategy, which one should it use?” HTTP intentionally leaves that decision open: as long as the identifier changes whenever the resource changes, the server is free to generate it however it likes. Over the years, four approaches have become common.

Production Note
Most CRUD APIs don’t hash their responses to build an ETag. They use a version number or an updated_at column, because comparing a single integer or timestamp is far cheaper than hashing a large response on every request.

Strategy 1 — Using a version number

Imagine your users table looks like this:

Users
─────────────────────────────────────
ID    Name      Followers    Version
─────────────────────────────────────
10    Tanzim    1284         37

Every time something about the user changes, the application increments the version — so after a profile update, Version = 37 becomes Version = 38. The server can simply use that version as the ETag:

ETag: "38"

No hashing, no extra computation. When the browser later sends If-None-Match: "38", the server only needs to compare two numbers. If they match, it returns 304 Not Modified; otherwise, 200 OK. This is one of the fastest and most common approaches for dynamic APIs, because the application already knows when the resource changes.

Strategy 2 — Using a timestamp

Some applications don’t keep a version column, but they already store when a record was last modified:

Users
────────────────────────────────────
ID    Name      Updated At
────────────────────────────────────
10    Tanzim    2026-07-21 10:42:18

The server can reuse that value directly:

ETag: "2026-07-21T10:42:18"

Whenever the record changes, the timestamp changes too. The browser doesn’t know it’s a timestamp, and it doesn’t need to — it simply stores the value and sends it back later.

Strategy 3 — Hashing the response

Sometimes the server doesn’t have a version number, or a timestamp isn’t reliable enough. In that case, it builds the response first and then calculates a hash of it:

JSON Response  ──▶  SHA-256  ──▶  "ab73f91c..."

That hash becomes the ETag:

ETag: "ab73f91c..."

If even one byte of the response changes, the hash changes, which makes hashes an excellent representation of the current version. The trade-off is that hashing large responses costs CPU time — we’ll come back to that.

Strategy 4 — File metadata

Static files work a little differently. Imagine you’re serving logo.png. The server already knows information about the file, such as its size (512 KB) and last-modified time (2026-07-21 09:15). Some web servers combine this metadata to produce an ETag, while others generate a hash of the file. Either approach works, because the browser never tries to interpret the value — it simply sends it back on the next request.

The browser doesn’t care which strategy you use

Here’s something worth noticing: each strategy generates a completely different ETag.

Version         "38"
Timestamp       "2026-07-21T10:42:18"
Hash            "ab73f91c..."
File metadata   "8f2-20260721"

From the browser’s perspective, they’re all identical. The browser never asks whether the value is a version number or a SHA-256 hash. It doesn’t inspect the value, and it doesn’t calculate anything. It follows one rule: receive the ETag, store it, and send it back later.

That’s why HTTP treats an ETag as an opaque identifier. The browser doesn’t need to understand it — only the server that created it knows what it means.

So which strategy should you choose? There isn’t a universal winner, because each one solves a different problem:

Version Number                    Timestamp
✅ Very fast                      ✅ Easy to implement
✅ Excellent for databases        ✅ Already exists in many tables
❌ Requires version tracking      ❌ Depends on timestamp precision
Hash                              File Metadata
✅ Represents the entire response ✅ Perfect for static files
✅ No extra database fields       ✅ Handled by many web servers
❌ More CPU intensive             ❌ Not useful for dynamic APIs

The important thing isn’t which strategy the server chooses. The important thing is that the same resource version always produces the same ETag, and a new resource version produces a different one. That’s the only promise HTTP needs.

This raises another question. If a website has one million users, does the server have to remember one million different ETags? Or can it remain completely stateless? That turns out to be one of the most elegant parts of the entire design.

Why Servers Stay Stateless

Let’s imagine your application suddenly becomes popular. Instead of ten users, you now have one million, and every browser requests the same profile endpoint. During the first request, every browser receives ETag: "v38".

A natural question appears: where is "v38" stored? Many developers imagine something like this:

Server Memory
User A  → v38
User B  → v38
User C  → v38
...
1,000,000 users

Every browser has its own record, and every request looks up that record. It sounds reasonable, but imagine what it would mean. Your server would need to remember every browser that has ever visited your website. If a browser closes its tab or loses its connection, the server would eventually need to clean up that memory. And if you ran ten application servers instead of one, every server would need exactly the same information. The system quickly becomes expensive, complicated, and difficult to scale.

Fortunately, HTTP doesn’t work this way. The server remembers nothing about individual browsers. Instead, the browser remembers the ETag, and the server only remembers the current state of the resource.

Browser                     Database
Cache                       User
├── Response Body           └── Version = 38
└── ETag: "v38"

That’s a very important distinction. The browser remembers “This is the version I have,” while the server only knows “This is the latest version that exists.” Nothing more.

Every request starts from scratch

This is one of the core ideas behind modern web servers: every HTTP request is treated as an independent conversation. The server processes a request, sends the response, and then completely forgets about it. A second later, when another request arrives, it’s a brand new conversation. The server doesn’t remember yesterday’s request, the previous browser, or the ETag it sent five seconds ago.

That’s exactly why the browser includes the If-None-Match header. Instead of saying "Remember what you sent me last time?", the browser says "This is the version I currently have." The server never has to remember anything, because the browser brings the information with it.

The server recreates the current version

When the request arrives, the server simply determines the current version of the resource again. Depending on the application, that might be a database version (38), an updated timestamp (2026-07-21 10:42), or a SHA-256 hash (ab73f91c...). Whatever the strategy, the process is always the same: read the current ETag, compare it against If-None-Match, and return 304 Not Modified if they're equal or 200 OK with a new response and ETag if they're not.

Notice something beautiful here. The browser remembers its version, and the server recreates the latest version. Neither side needs to remember previous conversations.

What “stateless” really means

People often hear the word stateless and think “the server stores no data.” That’s not true. The server obviously stores application data — your database still contains users, products, posts, and orders. What the server doesn’t store is client-specific conversation state. It doesn’t remember which browser requested the page, which ETag that browser received yesterday, or which responses were sent five minutes ago.

Every request contains everything the server needs:

HTTP Request
├── URL
├── Headers
├── Body (if any)
└── If-None-Match

The server processes that request, sends a response, and immediately forgets the conversation. That’s one of the reasons HTTP scales so well: any server can process any request because it doesn’t depend on what happened before.

So let’s return to our one million users. Do they require one million stored ETags? No. If they’re all requesting the same resource, they all receive the same identifier:

Resource: Current Version = 38
        │
        ├──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
        ▼              ▼              ▼              ▼
   Browser A       Browser B      Browser C      Browser D
   ETag: v38       ETag: v38      ETag: v38      ETag: v38

The server doesn’t create a unique ETag for each user. It creates one identity for one version of one resource, and every browser remembers that identity independently. That’s what makes the design elegant — the server scales because it doesn’t remember clients, and the browser participates by remembering its own version and presenting it again when it asks for the resource.

Engineering Insight
Stateless HTTP wasn’t designed because engineers dislike memory. It was designed so that any server can handle any request — which is exactly what makes horizontal scaling possible.

Recreating the ETag on every request instead of storing it raises a fair worry, though: doesn’t that mean rebuilding the whole response every time?

Imagine the browser sends GET /api/profile with If-None-Match: "v38". To compare the ETag, does the server have to read the entire database record, build the JSON response, calculate a new ETag, and only then compare it with "v38"? For a small response, that might not seem expensive. But what if the response is several megabytes, or your API handles 100,000 requests every second? Rebuilding every response just to discover nothing changed would waste a tremendous amount of CPU time.

Fortunately, well-designed systems rarely work that way.

The naive implementation

Let’s start with the simplest approach. The server reads the database, builds the JSON, generates a hash, compares it, and returns 304:

Browser: GET /profile, If-None-Match "v38"
        │
        ▼
Server: Read DB → Build JSON → Generate hash → Compare → 304

This works perfectly. But notice that the server did almost all of the work. It queried the database, serialized the response, and calculated the ETag, only to conclude “Nothing changed.”

For small applications, this is completely acceptable, and many frameworks do exactly this. As traffic grows, however, engineers begin asking a different question: can we determine whether the resource changed without rebuilding the entire response?

Look at the version, not the response

Imagine your database already stores a version number. When a request arrives, the server doesn’t need the complete profile immediately — first, it only needs one piece of information: the current version.

Browser: If-None-Match "38"
        │
        ▼
Server: Read version → 38 → Compare

If both versions match, the server immediately returns 304 Not Modified. Notice what never happened: no JSON serialization, no large response, no unnecessary network transfer. The server answered the question before doing the expensive work.

The same idea applies to timestamps. If the application stores an updated_at value and it hasn't changed, there's no reason to rebuild the response. Again, the expensive work is avoided.

Hash-based ETags are different

Hashing tells a different story. To calculate a hash, the server usually needs the complete response:

Database → Build JSON → SHA-256 → Compare

That produces a very accurate ETag, but it also requires more work. For static files, that’s rarely a problem. For very large dynamic responses, hashing on every request can become expensive — which is why many large applications prefer version numbers or timestamps for API responses.

Engineering is about avoiding unnecessary work

Notice what’s happening here. The browser isn’t the only system trying to save work — the server is doing exactly the same thing. Instead of asking “Can I build this response faster?”, it asks a better question: “Can I avoid building this response altogether?”

That’s one of the most valuable lessons in backend engineering: the fastest operation is often the one you never perform.

There’s no universally best strategy, because it depends on the resource. Small dynamic APIs are often ideal for version numbers or timestamps. Large static files work well with hashes. Generated documents may be simplest with a hash. Every strategy is trying to answer the same question — “Has this resource changed?” — and the only difference is how efficiently the application reaches that answer.

Generating ETags in Practice

Up to this point, we’ve talked about ETags as if you were building the server yourself. In reality, many developers never generate an ETag manually. They write something as simple as this:

res.json(user)

Yet when they inspect the response in the browser, they see:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "686897696a7c876b7e"

No code generated that value explicitly. So where did it come from? The answer is surprisingly simple: many frameworks include ETag generation as part of the response pipeline.

Think about what the framework already knows

Before a framework sends an HTTP response, it already has everything it needs. Consider a simple GET /api/profile endpoint. Internally, the request passes through several stages — router, controller, service, database — and produces a final JSON response:

{
  "id": 10,
  "name": "Tanzim",
  "followers": 1284
}

Before sending that response to the browser, the framework has one final opportunity to modify it. This is where many frameworks automatically generate an ETag:

Router → Controller → JSON Response → Generate ETag → HTTP Response

The application developer never sees this step. It happens internally.

How does the framework generate it?

Most general-purpose frameworks don’t understand your business logic. They don’t know whether your application uses version numbers, timestamps, event sourcing, or optimistic locking. All they see is the final response. So the simplest approach is to hash it:

JSON Response → Generate hash → ETag

That’s why frameworks like Express can generate ETags without asking your application for any additional information. They simply use the response they were already going to send.

This works because of something we learned earlier: the browser never tries to understand an ETag. It only checks whether the value changes. If the JSON changes from "followers": 1284 to "followers": 1285, the generated hash changes too, so the ETag changes, and the browser immediately knows it's looking at a new version.

Automatic doesn’t always mean optimal

Framework-generated ETags are a great default, and for many applications they’re more than enough. But think about what the framework had to do:

Database → Build JSON → Generate hash → Send response

Even if nothing changed, the framework still had to build the response before it could calculate the ETag. Earlier, we saw another approach: instead of rebuilding the entire response, the application can compare a simple version number and return 304 without serializing anything. That's why high-performance applications often replace the framework's default behavior with their own strategy.

So should the framework generate the ETag, or should your application? The answer depends on how much control you need:

Framework-generated ETags        Application-generated ETags
✔ Simple                         ✔ Full control
✔ Automatic                      ✔ Can use version numbers
✔ Great default                  ✔ Better for high-traffic APIs
✖ Limited optimization           ✖ More implementation work

Neither approach is universally better. For small and medium applications, automatic ETags are often the right choice. As systems grow, many teams switch to application-specific versioning because it avoids unnecessary work and fits their domain model better.

Now let’s write the actual code. We’ll use Node.js and Express, but the same three ideas apply to any language or framework: let the framework do it, take control with a version-based ETag, or verify the behavior with curl.

Option 1 — Let the framework do it

Express adds an ETag to most responses by default. You don’t have to write anything:

const express = require("express");
const app = express();


app.get("/api/profile", async (req, res) => {
  const user = await db.getUser(10);
  res.json(user); // Express generates a weak ETag from the response body
});

When the browser sends If-None-Match on the next request, Express compares it to the ETag it would generate for the new response, and returns 304 Not Modified automatically if they match. You can control this with a single setting:

app.set("etag", "strong"); // "weak" (default), "strong", or false to disable

This is the right choice for most small and medium applications. The only cost is that Express still builds the full response before it can hash it.

Option 2 — Take control with a version-based ETag

When you want to skip building the response entirely, generate the ETag yourself from a version column. This is the fast path we discussed earlier:

app.get("/api/profile", async (req, res) => {
  // Cheap query: read only the version, not the whole record
  const version = await db.getUserVersion(10);
  const etag = `"v${version}"`;



res.set("ETag", etag);
  // The browser's stored validator arrives in this header
  if (req.headers["if-none-match"] === etag) {
    return res.status(304).end(); // No body - reuse the cached copy
  }
  // Only now do the expensive work
  const user = await db.getUser(10);
  res.json(user);
});

Notice the ordering. The server reads a single version number, compares it, and returns 304 before touching the full record or serializing any JSON. On a hot endpoint, that difference is enormous.

One simplification to be aware of: a real If-None-Match header can contain a list of validators or the wildcard *. Production code should parse it rather than compare strings directly, but the idea is exactly the same.

Option 3 — Verify it works with curl

You don’t need a browser to see cache validation happen. First, make a normal request and look at the ETag header in the response:

curl -i https://api.example.com/api/profile

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "v37"
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":10,"name":"Tanzim","followers":1284}

Now send that ETag back with If-None-Match and watch the server skip the body:

curl -i -H 'If-None-Match: "v37"' https://api.example.com/api/profile

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
ETag: "v37"

No body, just a confirmation. You can see the same exchange in your browser’s DevTools under the Network tab — click any request and look for ETag in the response headers and If-None-Match in the request headers.

Strong ETags vs Weak ETags

Up to this point, we’ve treated every ETag as if it represented an exact version of a resource. That assumption works most of the time. But imagine these two responses. The first looks like this:

{
  "name": "Tanzim",
  "followers": 1284
}

The second looks like this:

{"name":"Tanzim","followers":1284}

If you compare them byte by byte, they’re different — the first contains spaces and line breaks, the second doesn’t. But if you’re building an application, do those formatting differences actually matter? Of course not. Both responses contain exactly the same information, the user sees the same profile, and the application behaves the same. The only thing that changed is how the JSON was formatted.

This introduces an interesting question. Should the browser download the entire response again just because a few spaces disappeared? Sometimes the answer is yes, and sometimes it’s no. That’s why HTTP defines two kinds of ETags.

Strong ETags

A strong ETag says: these two resources must be identical, byte for byte. If even a single byte changes, the ETag changes too.

Imagine a text file containing Hello World. If someone edits it to hello World, only one letter changed — but to a strong ETag, that's a completely different resource. Likewise, {"followers": 1284} and {"followers":1284} are different, because the bytes are different. A strong ETag treats every byte as significant.

You’ll usually see it written with no prefix, just the identifier:

ETag: "a8d92f..."

Strong ETags are the safest choice when the exact bytes matter — for downloadable files, PDFs, ZIP archives, images, videos, and API responses where every byte should match.

Weak ETags

Sometimes the exact bytes don’t matter — only the meaning does. Imagine these two HTML snippets:

<h1>Hello</h1>

and

<h1>
Hello
</h1>

The HTML renderer produces exactly the same page. Only the formatting changed, so downloading the entire page again doesn’t provide any real benefit. That’s where weak ETags become useful.

A weak ETag says: these resources are equivalent, even if they’re not byte-for-byte identical. It’s written with a W/ prefix:

ETag: W/"a8d92f..."

That tiny prefix completely changes the meaning. It tells the browser, “Treat these resources as the same for caching purposes, even if the raw bytes aren’t identical.”

Strong vs weak, side by side

Strong ETag                       Weak ETag
────────────────────────          ────────────────────────
Every byte must match.            Meaning must match.
Formatting change =               Formatting change =
different resource.               equivalent resource.
Asks: "Are the bytes              Asks: "Will this behave
exactly the same?"                the same for the client?"

Neither approach is “better” — they solve different problems. Strong validation asks “Are these bytes exactly the same?” Weak validation asks “Will this behave the same for the client?”

For most API responses, strong ETags are the default choice, because if the JSON changes even by one byte, the application usually wants the browser to receive the latest representation. Weak ETags become useful when the resource can change internally without changing what the user actually experiences. Many web servers also generate weak ETags automatically for certain resources, because they reduce unnecessary downloads caused by insignificant formatting differences.

The important lesson isn’t memorizing the W/ prefix. It's understanding what is being validated — sometimes exact bytes, sometimes equivalent content. HTTP supports both because different applications have different requirements.

Beyond Caching: Using ETags for Safe Updates

So far, every example has been about reading data. But ETags solve a second problem that has nothing to do with caching: preventing lost updates when two people edit the same resource at the same time.

Picture this. Alice and Bob both open the same profile, which is at version 37. Alice changes the bio and saves. A moment later, Bob — who still has the old version 37 open — changes the follower count and saves. Bob’s save is based on stale data, so it silently overwrites Alice’s change. Alice’s edit is gone, and nobody noticed.

Both load version 37
        │
   ┌────┴────┐
   ▼         ▼
 Alice      Bob
 edits bio  edits followers
   │         │
 saves →38   saves →38 (based on stale 37)
   │         │
   ▼         ▼
Alice's change is silently lost

This is called the lost update problem, and ETags fix it using a request header called If-Match. It's the mirror image of If-None-Match.

When the client sends an update, it includes the version it started from:

PUT /api/profile
If-Match: "v37"


{ "followers": 1285 }

The server only applies the change if the resource is still at version 37. If someone else already moved it to version 38, the precondition fails and the server refuses the write:

HTTP/1.1 412 Precondition Failed

Here’s the flow with two clients:

In code, the check is small:

app.put("/api/profile", async (req, res) => {
  const version = await db.getUserVersion(10);
  const currentEtag = `"v${version}"`;
  const clientEtag = req.headers["if-match"];

if (clientEtag && clientEtag !== currentEtag) {
    return res.status(412).end(); // Someone changed it first - refuse
  }
  const updated = await db.updateUser(10, req.body); // bumps version to 38
  res.set("ETag", `"v${updated.version}"`);
  res.json(updated);
});

When Bob receives the 412, his client re-fetches the latest version, shows him the current data, and lets him re-apply his change on top of Alice's. Nothing is lost.

This pattern is called optimistic concurrency control. It’s “optimistic” because it assumes conflicts are rare and only checks at save time, instead of locking the resource while someone edits it. The same ETag that saves bandwidth on reads doubles as a conflict detector on writes — which is exactly why strong ETags matter here: for a safe write, you usually want an exact-version match, not an “equivalent” one.

ETag, Last-Modified, and Cache-Control

ETags don’t work alone. Two other HTTP headers show up constantly alongside them, and it’s worth knowing how they fit together.

Last-Modified is the other validator

Before ETags, HTTP already had a way to validate a cached copy: the Last-Modified timestamp. The server sends when the resource last changed, and the browser sends it back on the next request using If-Modified-Since:

Response:  Last-Modified: Tue, 21 Jul 2026 10:42:18 GMT
Request:   If-Modified-Since: Tue, 21 Jul 2026 10:42:18 GMT

If the resource hasn’t changed since that time, the server returns 304 Not Modified, exactly like with an ETag.

So why do ETags exist if Last-Modified already does the job? Because timestamps are coarse. They usually have one-second resolution, so a resource that changes twice in the same second looks unchanged. And some resources have no meaningful "modified time" at all. An ETag can represent any version — a hash, a counter, a revision — with byte-level precision. When both headers are present, ETags take priority.

Cache-Control decides whether to even ask

There’s a subtle point hiding in everything above. Validation still requires a network round trip — the browser asks “is my copy still good?” and waits for 304. But sometimes you don't want it to ask at all.

That’s what Cache-Control is for. It controls freshness: how long the browser may reuse a copy without contacting the server.

Cache-Control: max-age=60

For 60 seconds, the browser treats its copy as fresh and serves it instantly — zero requests. After 60 seconds the copy becomes stale, and now the browser revalidates using If-None-Match, getting back either a 304 or a fresh response.

max-age window          after max-age
──────────────          ─────────────
Serve from cache        Revalidate with If-None-Match
No request at all       → 304 (reuse) or 200 (new copy)

So the two concepts are complementary. Cache-Control answers "do I even need to ask?" and the ETag answers "since I'm asking, has it changed?" A common, effective pattern is a short max-age for instant repeat loads, backed by an ETag so that revalidation stays cheap when the window expires.

Everything so far has assumed one browser talking to one server. Real production systems rarely look like that. A request might pass through a CDN, a reverse proxy, a load balancer, and multiple application servers, and sometimes it even reaches a database in another region. If the browser sends the same ETag to a completely different server, how does that server know whether it’s still valid? That’s where HTTP cache validation meets distributed systems.

ETags in Distributed Systems

Up to this point, our architecture has been wonderfully simple. Every request followed exactly the same path:

Browser → Application Server → Database

The browser requested a resource, the application generated an ETag, and the browser stored it. On the next request, the server generated the current ETag again, compared the two values, and decided whether to return 304 Not Modified or a fresh response. Everything worked beautifully, and this architecture is enough for many applications.

But successful applications rarely stay small forever. Imagine your API starts becoming popular. At first, a hundred users send a request every few seconds and your server handles it without any problems. A few months later, ten thousand users send thousands of requests every minute. CPU usage starts climbing, memory usage increases, and response times become inconsistent. Then one day your monitoring dashboard shows CPU at 98%, memory at 91%, and response times that have jumped from 80 ms to 1.8 s.

The application hasn’t become slower because ETags stopped working. It has become slower because one machine has reached its limits. No matter how powerful a server is, it has finite resources: a limited number of CPU cores, a limited amount of memory, and limited network bandwidth. Eventually, every server reaches a point where it simply cannot process any more requests.

At that moment, engineers almost always make the same decision: “Let’s add another server.” So instead of a single application server, you put a load balancer in front of several:

At first glance, nothing seems to change. The browser still sends GET /api/profile, the application still returns ETag: "v38", and the browser still sends If-None-Match: "v38". Everything should continue working exactly as before. Or should it?

Think about the last request. The browser received ETag: "v38" from Server A. But the next request doesn't necessarily go back to Server A — the load balancer might choose Server B or Server C instead. Now ask yourself a simple question: how does Server C know that "v38" is still the correct ETag?

Remember, HTTP servers are stateless. Server C has never seen this browser before, it wasn’t the server that generated the original response, and it doesn’t remember the previous conversation. So how can it confidently reply with 304 Not Modified instead of sending the entire response again?

That single question marks the beginning of a much bigger topic. We’ve understood how one browser talks to one server. Now we need to understand how the same conversation continues when there are many servers, load balancers, and eventually databases spread across the world.

Why stateless HTTP makes load balancing possible

The browser received ETag: "v38" from Server A. A few seconds later, the user refreshes, but this time the load balancer sends the request to Server B. The browser still sends exactly the same request:

GET /api/profile
If-None-Match: "v38"

Server B has never seen this browser before. It didn’t generate the previous response, and it never sent "v38". So how can it possibly know whether "v38" is still the latest version?

At first, this feels like a serious problem. Many developers assume Server B must somehow ask Server A, “Hey, did you send ETag v38 to this browser yesterday?” Or perhaps all the servers share a giant table mapping users to ETags. But neither approach works. Imagine hundreds of application servers, millions of users, and thousands of requests every second. Keeping every server synchronized with every browser’s cache state would quickly become more expensive than simply sending the response again.

Fortunately, HTTP solves the problem in a much simpler way: Server B doesn’t need to know what Server A sent.

That sounds strange at first, but remember something we learned earlier. The browser isn’t asking “What did Server A send me?” It’s asking “I currently have Version 38. Is Version 38 still the latest?” That changes everything, because the request already contains all the information Server B needs:

GET /api/profile
If-None-Match: "v38"

Server B doesn’t need Server A. It doesn’t need shared memory, and it doesn’t need a session. It only needs one piece of information: “What is the current version of this resource?” If the database still says Version = 38, then Server B reaches exactly the same conclusion that Server A would have reached, and it replies with 304 Not Modified.

Notice what just happened. The browser talked to two completely different application servers, yet the conversation continued as if it were speaking to the same machine. That’s only possible because HTTP is stateless — every request contains everything the server needs to process it. No previous conversation has to be remembered, and no application server has to know which server handled the previous request. The browser carries the conversation forward by sending the ETag back with every request, and the application server simply validates it against the current version of the resource.

This is one of the reasons HTTP scales so well. Adding another server doesn’t require sharing millions of client sessions, because any server can process any request when every request is self-contained.

Once you understand this, something else becomes obvious. All three application servers reached the same answer because they all read from the same database. But what happens when there isn’t just one database anymore? What happens when your application grows beyond a single region and different servers begin reading from different databases? That’s where a new challenge appears — one that HTTP alone cannot solve.

When databases stop agreeing: replication lag

In the previous section, every application server behaved the same way. It didn’t matter whether the request reached Server A, B, or C, because they all read from the same database and generated the same ETag:

As long as every server agrees on the current version of the resource, ETags work exactly as we expect. But successful systems don’t stop here.

Imagine your application now serves users around the world — in Asia, Europe, and North America. Every request still travels to a single database. For users close to the database, everything feels fast. For users on the other side of the world, every request spends hundreds of milliseconds crossing continents before it even reaches the database. As traffic grows, that latency becomes noticeable, and soon another architectural decision appears: “Let’s place databases closer to our users.”

Now the architecture changes again:

At first glance, this looks like a huge improvement. Users in Asia read from Asia, users in Europe read from Europe, and everyone gets lower latency. But a new problem quietly appears. Unlike application servers, databases contain state.

If Alice updates her profile in Asia, the Asia database becomes Version = 39. How does Europe know? Nothing magical happens — the change must travel across the network through replication, and that takes time. Sometimes it's a few milliseconds, sometimes hundreds, sometimes longer. During that short period, the two databases temporarily disagree:

Asia Database        Europe Database
Version = 39         Version = 38

Both databases are temporarily correct from their own perspective. One has already received the update, and the other hasn’t.

Now let’s follow a real request. Earlier, the browser visited Asia and received ETag: "39", which it stored. A few seconds later, the next request reaches Europe instead:

GET /api/profile
If-None-Match: "39"

Europe checks its own database, where the current version is still 38. Comparing the two values, 39 (browser) does not equal 38 (Europe). Europe concludes that the browser's copy is outdated, so it returns:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "38"

Wait. The browser already had the newer version. Why did it receive an older one? Did ETag fail?

No. The ETag worked perfectly. The browser honestly reported “I have Version 39,” and Europe honestly answered “The latest version I know about is Version 38.” The disagreement wasn’t caused by HTTP — it was caused by the databases temporarily disagreeing about reality. This is called replication lag, and it’s one of the most important ideas in distributed systems.

Engineering Insight
The ETag didn’t fail. The databases disagreed. Cache validation only ever reports what one server believes is current — it can’t paper over an inconsistency that lives one layer below it.

An ETag simply reports what this server believes is the latest version. It doesn’t synchronize databases, it doesn’t replicate data, and it doesn’t solve distributed consistency. It only validates the current version that the server can see. This is a subtle but incredibly important distinction. Many engineers encounter this situation for the first time and think “ETags are broken.” They’re not — the cache validation protocol is behaving exactly as designed. What’s changing is the architecture underneath it.

We’ve crossed a boundary. Until now, every question belonged to HTTP. From this point onward, the questions belong to distributed systems: How quickly should databases replicate? Should every region wait for every other region before accepting writes? Is temporary inconsistency acceptable? Those decisions determine what every server believes is the “current” version of a resource.

And once you realize that, you also realize something else: ETags were never the hard part. The hard part is ensuring that every server sees the same version of reality.

Here is the whole journey in one picture — a validation request travelling through a real production stack, from the browser all the way to a replicated database, and the 304 that comes back when every layer agrees:

Every layer is stateless except the database, and every layer reaches the same answer only because the version it reads agrees. The ETag is the thread that ties the whole path together.

Common Mistakes and Pitfalls

ETags are simple in principle, but a few real-world details trip up almost everyone at least once. Here are the ones worth knowing before you ship.

Five misconceptions to unlearn

Before the operational gotchas, clear up the ideas that cause the most confusion:

  • “An ETag is always a SHA hash.” No — it can be a version number, a timestamp, or any opaque token. A hash is just one option.
  • “The server stores each browser’s ETag.” No — the browser stores it and sends it back. The server only knows the current version.
  • “An ETag is a cache.” No — it’s a validator for a cache. Cache-Control decides whether to cache; the ETag decides whether the cached copy is still valid.
  • “Enable ETags on everything.” No — they only help for resources read repeatedly without changing. On always-changing endpoints they add work for nothing.
  • “Cache-Control and ETag do the same job.” No — Cache-Control controls freshness (whether to ask at all); the ETag controls validation (whether the copy is still current once you do ask).

Compression can silently change your ETag

Most servers compress responses with gzip or Brotli. If a strong ETag is computed from the compressed bytes, then the same resource can produce different ETags depending on whether — and how — it was compressed. A client that got the gzipped version and a proxy that got the identity version end up disagreeing.

This is one reason servers so often emit weak ETags for compressible content, or compute the ETag from the original content before compression. If you generate ETags yourself, hash the underlying resource, not the encoded output.

Hashing must be deterministic across every server

Remember the load balancer. If you use hash-based ETags, every server must produce the same hash for the same resource, or validation breaks the moment a request lands on a different machine. That sounds obvious, but it fails quietly when the serialization isn’t stable — for example, a JSON object whose keys come out in a different order on different runs, or a hash that includes a timestamp or a random value.

The fix is to hash a canonical form: sort keys, exclude volatile fields, and make sure the input is identical everywhere. A version number or updated_at column sidesteps the problem entirely, which is part of why large systems favor them.

Proxies and CDNs sit in the middle

A CDN or reverse proxy may cache, revalidate, or even strip validators on your behalf. That’s usually helpful — a CDN can answer 304 at the edge without touching your origin — but it means the ETag your code sends isn't always the one the browser sees. When something looks wrong, inspect the response at each hop, not just at the origin.

ETags can be abused for tracking

Because a browser stores an ETag and sends it back automatically, a server can assign each visitor a unique ETag and use it to re-identify them later — even after they clear cookies. These “ETag supercookies” have been used for tracking, and browsers and privacy regulations have pushed back on the practice.

The lesson: an ETag should identify a resource version, never a user. If your ETags encode anything per-visitor, that’s a red flag.

When Should You Use ETags?

After everything we’ve explored, one practical question remains: should every API use ETags? The short answer is no. ETags are useful only when the same resource is requested repeatedly and there’s a reasonable chance it hasn’t changed. If every request always returns brand-new data, validating a cached copy provides little value.

A good candidate

Consider a profile endpoint:

GET /api/profile

Most users refresh their profile several times, and in many cases nothing changes between those requests. An ETag lets the browser reuse the existing response instead of downloading the same JSON again. The same idea applies to blog articles, product pages, user settings, documentation, images, CSS, and JavaScript bundles. These resources change occasionally, but they’re read far more often than they’re updated — which is exactly where ETags shine.

A poor candidate

Now consider an endpoint like this:

GET /api/random-number

Every request generates a new value, so even if the browser sends an ETag, the response will always be different and every request becomes a 200 OK. The cache is never reused, and the ETag provides almost no benefit. The same is true for endpoints that intentionally return different data every time — random values, current server time, live stock prices, or rapidly changing metrics. In these cases, validation simply adds extra work without reducing network traffic.

Static files

For static assets like logo.png, styles.css, and app.js, ETags are almost always a good idea. These files change infrequently, and when they do change, browsers should immediately download the new version. Most web servers and CDNs already generate ETags automatically for these resources, so in many applications you never need to think about them.

Dynamic APIs

Dynamic APIs require a little more thought. Suppose you’re returning user information with GET /api/users/10. If your application already maintains a version number or an updated_at column, generating an ETag is usually inexpensive. But if generating an ETag requires rebuilding a very large response and hashing it on every request, you should consider whether a version-based approach would be more efficient. The right choice depends on how your application already tracks changes.

Don’t enable ETags just because you can

This is a common mistake. Developers discover that their framework supports automatic ETags, so they enable them for every endpoint. That isn’t always the right decision. Ask yourself one simple question: is this resource likely to be requested multiple times without changing? If the answer is yes, an ETag can reduce unnecessary work. If the answer is no, cache validation probably isn’t buying you much. Engineering isn’t about enabling every feature — it’s about solving the right problem.

The Mental Model to Remember

If you forget everything else from this handbook, remember this: an ETag is not a cache. It isn’t a hash, and it isn’t a version number. Those are only possible implementations. The real idea is much simpler.

Every time a browser requests a resource, two independent systems need to answer one question:

“Are we both looking at the same version of this resource?”

If the answer is yes, HTTP sends 304 Not Modified. If the answer is no, HTTP sends 200 OK along with the latest representation and a new ETag.

Everything we’ve discussed — from browser caching to framework internals, from stateless servers to globally distributed systems — is simply a different way of answering that one question efficiently. That’s why ETags have remained part of HTTP for decades. They’re not a clever optimization. They’re a simple, elegant protocol for establishing agreement between two systems that never assu me they remember each other.

The HTTP ETags Handbook: How Browsers Know a File Hasn’t Changed Without Re-Downloading It was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Build an Agentic Software Factory!
partialText:
The term software factory is getting a lot of attention right now, and for a good reason. AI coding assistants can generate code much faster than before. But faster coding alone does not mean faster, safer delivery. In many teams, it simply moves the bottleneck to review, testing, deployment, and operations.

A software factory is a way to organize the entire software development life cycle as one connected, repeatable system. Think of a car manufacturing assembly line. Each station has a clear job, work moves forward in a predictable order, quality checks happen at the right moments, and the finished product is inspected before it leaves the factory.

An agentic software factory applies that same idea to software delivery. AI agents do focused work across planning, coding, testing, deployment, monitoring, and feedback. Humans remain in charge of specifications, security, policies, approvals, and the decisions that should never be delegated blindly.

Key Takeaways

  • An agentic software factory coordinates AI agents across the complete software delivery lifecycle.
  • Faster AI-assisted coding can create review bottlenecks unless downstream stages also improve.
  • Humans retain ownership by defining guardrails, specifications, approvals, and security requirements.
  • Workflow orchestration connects context, automation, observability, incident handling, and feedback loops.

What Is a Software Factory?

A software factory is not just a collection of developer tools. It is an operating model where software delivery is designed as a smooth, observable workflow from idea to production and back into improvement.

In a car factory, a vehicle moves through assembly, painting, quality inspection, final assembly, and delivery. People are involved at important checkpoints, but the process does not restart from scratch at every station. It is structured, repeatable, and connected.

The same model works for software. In an agentic software factory, the flow can look like this:

  • Requirements and design: clarify what needs to be built and collect service context.
  • Planning: turn requirements into a feasible implementation plan.
  • Build: generate or modify code for a feature or bug fix.
  • Testing and continuous integration: validate the change and stop failures early.
  • Human review: approve, reject, or request changes before a risky next step.
  • Deployment: deliver the approved change through continuous delivery.
  • Monitoring and operations: check service health, create incidents, notify teams, and roll back when needed.
  • Feedback loop: feed production signals and outcomes back into future planning.

The important point is simple: agents perform work, while humans provide the gates. A software factory is not about removing people from the loop. It is about putting people at the moments where their judgment matters most.

How Software Delivery Evolved Into the Software Factory Model

The software factory did not appear suddenly. It is the next step in a long evolution toward more reliable software delivery.

From manual deployment to automated delivery

In the 1990s, developers often wrote the code, prepared servers, and deployed software manually. A release could take weeks or months. Testing and deployment were labor-intensive, and repeatability depended heavily on individual knowledge.

Then continuous integration tools such as Hudson and Jenkins helped teams automate builds and tests. The rise of DevOps brought development and operations closer together, reducing the handoff gap between teams. Continuous delivery, continuous deployment, and infrastructure as code tools such as Terraform pushed automation further.

GitOps and platforms such as Docker and Kubernetes added a strong operational model where Git could serve as the source of truth for application and infrastructure changes. Each stage made delivery more repeatable.

From automation to agentic engineering

After AI agents and coding assistants became practical, teams began using them across more parts of the SDLC. An agent could help gather requirements, propose a plan, write code, prepare tests, review pull requests, monitor a service, or summarize feedback.

That is where the software factory becomes agentic. Instead of treating AI as a single chat window or code completion tool, I treat it as a coordinated group of specialized workers inside a governed delivery system.

The software factory model gives those agents a place, a sequence, boundaries, and clear outputs. Without that structure, adding more agents can create more confusion rather than more throughput.

Why AI Coding Assistants Create New Bottlenecks

Before coding assistants, the time required across planning, coding, review, and shipping was comparatively balanced. Writing code often took a large part of the cycle, but every stage had its own workload.

Now coding can accelerate dramatically. Tools such as Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Codex can help teams generate and change code faster. The problem is that the rest of the system does not automatically become faster.

When code arrives faster, code review queues can become overloaded. Senior engineers get stuck reviewing a growing number of pull requests. Testing may become backed up. Deployment approvals may take longer. Only a small portion of the increased output may actually reach production.

This is exactly why a software factory matters. It looks at the whole system, not only the coding stage. A good software factory improves the flow across the entire lifecycle so that one accelerated step does not jam everything downstream.

Preventing agentic chaos

There is another issue. Developers are already using many tools across the SDLC. Add multiple AI agents without a common operating layer, and it becomes difficult to answer basic questions:

  • Which agent changed this service?
  • What context did the agent use?
  • Which policy or guardrail applied?
  • Who approved the deployment?
  • What should happen if the health check fails?

That is agentic chaos: lots of autonomous activity, but little visibility, control, governance, or accountable decision-making. A software factory makes the agent workflow explicit. It creates a visible path for work, controls access to actions, and places checks before high-impact changes.

Humans Still Own the System

It is tempting to say that an agentic software factory can automate everything end to end. Technically, many tasks can be automated. In reality, giving unrestricted authority to agents is risky. A poorly constrained agent can make the wrong decision, trigger the wrong action, or cause damage in production.

Humans and developers still own the system. In a well-designed software factory, my role is not to manually do every repeated task. My role is to define the rules of the factory.

That includes:

  • Defining product requirements and technical specifications.
  • Setting security checklists and guardrails.
  • Deciding which actions agents may take automatically.
  • Creating human approval gates for important decisions.
  • Reviewing plans, pull requests, release readiness, and incident responses.
  • Maintaining accountability for production systems.

This is the right division of responsibility. Agents can gather context, plan work, implement changes, run tests, check health, and notify teams. Developers decide what good looks like, which risks are acceptable, and whether a change should proceed.

The Building Blocks of an Agentic Software Factory

A practical software factory breaks broad lifecycle phases into smaller, focused responsibilities. Rather than relying on one giant agent to do everything, I can use agents for specific jobs and connect them through workflow orchestration.

Plan

The planning stage starts with human input and service context. A requirements agent can gather the feature request, identify the affected service, and collect relevant information. A planning agent can then turn that into an implementation plan. A feedback digest or product improvement agent can provide useful context from previous issues and outcomes.

Build and review

The build stage can include a feature builder and bug-fixer agent. The review stage can include a pull request reviewer, automated CI checks, and other quality actions. The key is that a failed CI build blocks the workflow. It should not quietly move toward deployment.

After CI succeeds, a human review gate can decide whether the change is ready to continue. This is where the software factory protects speed with judgment.

Deploy and operate

After approval, a continuous delivery agent can deploy the service or feature. A monitoring agent can then assess the health of the service. If health is degraded or a critical issue appears, the workflow can create an incident, notify the relevant team through Slack, and, where appropriate, perform an automated rollback.

The final piece is the feedback loop. Production data should not disappear into dashboards. It should update service context and help inform future planning. That loop is what turns a set of automation steps into an evolving software factory.

Building a Software Factory Workflow with Port

To put this into practice, I used Port as the context layer for an agentic SDLC. Port brings together workflow orchestration, agent management, service context, and governance so I can automate delivery without losing control.

Inside the platform, I can create services, agents, dashboards, self-service actions, and workflows. The workflow is the backbone of the software factory because it makes the entire path visible and enforceable.

Here is the workflow I built for a software factory agentic SDLC:

  1. Fetch service context: identify what the selected service is, its ownership, and relevant details.
  2. Gather requirements: use a requirements agent to understand the feature request.
  3. Create a plan: have a planning agent prepare the implementation approach.
  4. Build the change: use a coding agent to implement the requested work.
  5. Test and run CI: validate the change through testing and continuous integration.
  6. Block failures: stop the workflow immediately if CI fails.
  7. Request human review: let a developer approve or reject progression to deployment.
  8. Deploy through CD: release the approved change with a continuous delivery agent.
  9. Monitor health: inspect the health of the deployed service.
  10. Respond to degradation: create incidents, notify the right team, and roll back when required.
  11. Collect feedback: send outcomes back into the service catalog and planning context.
  12. Use a final deploy gate: keep a human decision point before final release or publishing.

I can trigger this software factory through self-service by choosing a service and describing a feature, such as adding an API gateway to a fraud detection service. The workflow begins by retrieving context, then moves through requirements, planning, code generation, testing, CI, review, deployment, and monitoring.

I can also trigger the workflow through Port AI. For example, I can request an agentic SDLC pipeline for a service and ask to add OpenTelemetry distributed tracing. The system can locate the service, find the appropriate software factory workflow, trigger it, and provide a live path to track the run.

That does not mean the workflow is a black box. I can inspect its stages, check the run state, see whether it is currently planning, coding, or testing, and review the workflow configuration. The software factory becomes both automated and observable.

Build Your Own Software Factory

Start Small, Then Expand the Factory

You do not need to automate every part of delivery on day one. A software factory can begin with one valuable and repeatable path. For example, start with requirements, coding, CI, and a human review gate. Once that flow is stable, add deployment automation, monitoring, incident creation, rollback rules, and feedback loops.

The goal is not automation for its own sake. The goal is a better system for delivering software: faster where tasks are repetitive, safer where risks are high, and clearer at every stage.

A mature software factory gives every agent a defined responsibility, every workflow a visible path, and every human a meaningful control point. That is how I can take advantage of agentic engineering without turning the SDLC into chaos.
